questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The clause that governs federal property
questions.learningObjective: state what the property clause authorises
questions.stem: One clause of the Constitution addresses the territory and other property belonging to the United States. What does it provide?

options.text: That Congress may dispose of it and make all needful rules and regulations respecting it
That the President may dispose of it by agreement with any state in which it lies
options.misconception: gives the disposal power to the President

options.text: That Congress must dispose of it within a fixed period or it reverts to the state
options.misconception: invents a reversion period that the clause does not state

options.text: That only the judiciary may make rules and regulations for the use of it
options.misconception: gives the rulemaking power to the judiciary

questions.explanation: The clause gives the Congress power to dispose of and to make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States. The two verbs are what the clause is for, and they are joined, so a disposal and a rule may stand or fall together or separately. The clause names the Congress, which disposes of the second option's answer, and it says nothing about any period after which land would revert, so the third option is excluded as well. The fourth option takes the rulemaking away from the body the clause names and gives it to the courts, which have no general authority to make rules for federal property at all. The clause also ends with a proviso that nothing in the Constitution is to be construed to prejudice the claims of the United States or of a particular state, so the property power sits alongside an express reservation about boundary claims.
questions.hint: Look for the two verbs the clause gives to one institution.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the property clause does not reach
questions.learningObjective: identify a dispute the property clause does not decide
questions.stem: The property clause is about territory and property belonging to the United States. Which of these is outside its subject matter?

options.text: A private dispute between two landowners over the boundary between their own parcels
options.misconception: treats a private boundary quarrel as federal property

options.text: The sale of federal land in a territory to a settler under a land law
options.misconception: denies that a land sale is within the property power

options.text: The rules governing the use of federal land leased to a grazier
options.misconception: denies that rules for use of federal land are within the property power

options.text: A boundary dispute between the United States and one of the states over land the United States claims

questions.explanation: The clause covers property belonging to the United States, and it says expressly that nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular state, so a claim about federal land is exactly the kind of thing the closing proviso is about and the kind of thing the opening words reach. Sale of federal land and rules for its use are the two verbs in the clause, so the third and fourth options are squarely inside it. A quarrel between two private landowners about the line between their own parcels involves no federal property at all, and the resolution of such a dispute is a matter for the ordinary courts under ordinary law rather than for the property power, which is the whole content of the second option's error.
questions.hint: Ask whether federal property is involved in the dispute at all.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cap on the seat-of-government district
questions.learningObjective: compute the area that the constitutional cap allows
questions.stem: The Constitution authorises Congress to legislate over a district ceded by the states for the seat of the government, not exceeding ten miles square. Using the survey convention of six hundred and forty acres to a square mile, what is the largest area that cap allows?

options.text: Ten square miles, which is six thousand four hundred acres
options.misconception: reads ten miles square as ten square miles

options.text: One hundred square miles, which is six hundred and forty thousand acres
options.misconception: carries the figure for one section across a hundred sections

options.text: One hundred square miles, which is sixty-four thousand acres
Twenty square miles, which is twelve thousand eight hundred acres
options.misconception: doubles the side instead of squaring it

questions.explanation: Ten miles square is a square ten miles on each side, so its area is ten multiplied by ten, which is one hundred square miles. At six hundred and forty acres to a square mile, one hundred square miles is one hundred times six hundred and forty, which is sixty-four thousand acres. The first option therefore has both the square miles and the acres right. The second option has doubled the side instead of squaring it, and the third has read the cap as though ten miles square meant ten square miles. The fourth option has the square miles right and the acres wrong by a factor of ten, which is the error of carrying over the figure for a single section as though it were the figure for a hundred of them.
questions.hint: Square the side, then convert square miles into acres using six hundred and forty to the square mile.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Buying land for a fort with a state's consent
questions.learningObjective: state the condition on federal purchase of land inside a state
questions.stem: The same clause that names the seat-of-government district also speaks of places purchased inside a state. What condition does it attach to such a purchase?

options.text: The purchase must be confirmed by a vote of two thirds in each house of the national legislature
options.misconception: invents a two-thirds approval rule the clause does not contain

options.text: The purchase must be made with the consent of the legislature of the state in which the place lies
The purchase requires only the consent of the governor of the state
options.misconception: substitutes the governor for the state legislature

options.text: The purchase is free of any state role, because the need is a national one
options.misconception: treats the written consent condition as absent

questions.explanation: The clause speaks of like authority over all places purchased by the consent of the legislature of the state in which the same shall be, for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dock-yards, and other needful buildings, and the consent of the state legislature is therefore written into the power. The named uses are military and naval ones, which is why the clause is part of the defence and property provisions rather than a general purchase power. The second option substitutes the governor for the legislature, which the words do not do, and the third option treats a written condition as though it were absent. The fourth option invents a supermajority rule that the clause does not contain, and no approval of a purchase is required by the clause at all, only the consent of the state.
questions.hint: Ask which body of the state must consent and for what listed purpose.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The bar on forming a state inside another
questions.learningObjective: state the two limits on forming a new state
questions.stem: One clause of the Constitution says when new states may be admitted and when they may not be formed. What does it forbid?

options.text: Forming a new state within the jurisdiction of another state without the consent of the legislatures concerned and of Congress
Forming a new state from parts of two states, whatever the consents of the legislatures concerned
options.misconception: drops the consents the clause requires for a junction of states

options.text: Admitting a new state without the consent of the legislature of every existing state
options.misconception: invents a consent from every existing state

options.text: Forming a new state out of a territory unless the territory has been surveyed into townships
options.misconception: invents a survey condition for the admission of a state

questions.explanation: The clause provides that new states may be admitted by the Congress, but that no new state shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other state, nor any state formed by the junction of two or more states, or parts of states, without the consent of the legislatures of the states concerned as well as of the Congress. Two conditions of consent are named and both are required, which is why the first option is right. The second option drops the consents for the junction case, which the clause expressly requires, and the third option invents a consent from every existing state, which the clause does not ask for. The fourth option invents a survey condition for admission, and the survey system of 1785 was a rule for the disposal of land rather than a gateway to statehood.
questions.hint: Read the whole sentence: it names two ways a state might be formed and one set of consents.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The third limb of the commerce clause
questions.learningObjective: identify the third subject of the commerce power
questions.stem: The commerce clause in Article I ends with a third subject after foreign nations and the several states. What is it?

options.text: Trade between the several states and the District of Columbia
options.misconception: invents a territorial subject the clause does not name

options.text: The granting of patents and copyrights for a limited time
options.misconception: confuses the copyright clause with the commerce clause

options.text: The sale of public lands to settlers in the territories
options.misconception: mistakes a commerce clause for the property power

options.text: Trade with the Indian tribes

questions.explanation: The clause authorises Congress to regulate commerce with foreign nations, and among the several states, and with the Indian tribes, and the third limb is the one that concerns the tribes. The list matters because each limb marks out a distinct subject, and the third is the one that has been read as a basis for a much wider congressional authority over affairs involving the tribes than the words of a commerce regulation would suggest, which is the whole of the argument in the fourth option and in the framing of the second. The third limb is not a grant of land, so the fourth option mistakes a clause about commerce for the property power, and the second option invents a territorial subject the clause does not name.
questions.hint: The three subjects stand in a list; find the third.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The township of the 1785 survey system
questions.learningObjective: state the unit of survey and how it is divided
questions.stem: The federal survey system of 1785 divides land into townships. How is a township laid out?

options.text: As a strip ten miles wide running north to south, with numbered ranges across it
options.misconception: describes ranges rather than townships

options.text: As a square one mile on a side, which is the unit later called a township
options.misconception: confuses a township with a section

options.text: As a square six miles on a side, marked out by north-south and east-west lines meeting at right angles
As a square seven miles on a side, following the first draft of the ordinance
options.misconception: reports a figure from a draft of the ordinance rather than the enacted text

questions.explanation: The ordinance of 1785 directed that the territory be divided into townships six miles square, by lines running due north and south and others crossing these at right angles, and that the plats be marked into sections of one mile square, or six hundred and forty acres. A township is therefore six miles on a side, and the one-mile square is the section inside it, which disposes of the fourth option. The second option is a real historical detail rather than a fiction, because a seven-mile township appeared in an earlier draft and was changed to six miles before the ordinance passed, so a reader who meets the seven-mile figure in a draft is not looking at the enacted text. The third option describes a different arrangement, in which the strips are called ranges and are numbered, rather than the townships themselves.
questions.hint: Ask how many miles a side and how many sections a township contains.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The acreage of a township and a section
questions.learningObjective: compute the acreage of a township from the survey convention
questions.stem: In the federal survey system a township is six miles square and is divided into sections of one mile square, each of six hundred and forty acres. How many acres does a whole township contain, and how many sections is that?

options.text: Twenty-three thousand and forty acres, in six hundred and forty sections
options.misconception: mistakes the acreage of a section for a count of sections

options.text: Twenty-three thousand and forty acres, in thirty-six sections
Twenty-three thousand and forty acres, in six sections
options.misconception: takes the side length for the number of sections

options.text: Three thousand eight hundred and forty acres, in thirty-six sections
options.misconception: divides by six instead of multiplying

questions.explanation: A township six miles on a side contains six times six, which is thirty-six square miles, and a one-mile square section is six hundred and forty acres, so the township contains thirty-six times six hundred and forty, which is twenty-three thousand and forty acres. Both halves of the first option follow, and the thirty-six sections are the same thirty-six square miles laid out one to a section. The second option takes the side length for the number of sections, which is the classic slip when a reader is given both a six-mile figure and a one-mile figure. The third option divides by six rather than multiplying, and the fourth option mistakes the acreage of a section for a count of sections.
questions.hint: Square the side to get square miles, then multiply by the acreage of one section.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The sections reserved in each township
questions.learningObjective: count the reserved sections and the share of a township they take
questions.stem: In each township of the survey system four sections were set aside before the rest were sold, namely sections eight, eleven, sixteen, and twenty-nine. Out of the thirty-six sections in a township, how many were reserved, what share of the township is that, and how many acres of six hundred and forty to a section do they come to?

options.text: Four sections, which is one ninth of the township and two thousand five hundred and sixty acres
Five sections, which is one seventh of the township and three thousand two hundred acres
options.misconception: counts five reserved sections and reaches one seventh

options.text: Four sections, which is one ninth of the township and one thousand two hundred and eighty acres
options.misconception: halves the acreage as though the sections were half-sections

options.text: Three sections, which is one twelfth of the township and one thousand nine hundred and twenty acres
options.misconception: counts three reserved sections and divides by twelve

questions.explanation: The reserved numbers are eight, eleven, sixteen, and twenty-nine, which is four sections out of the thirty-six, so the share is four thirty-sixths, which reduces to one ninth. At six hundred and forty acres to a section, four sections come to four times six hundred and forty, which is two thousand five hundred and sixty acres. The first option therefore has the count, the share, and the acreage all right, and the share is worth checking separately because one ninth and one twelfth are the two fractions a reader is most likely to produce. The second option counts five and reaches one seventh, which no reserved list supports. The third option halves the acreage as though the reserved sections were half-sections. The fourth option counts three and divides by twelve.
questions.hint: Count the reserved numbers, reduce the fraction against thirty-six, then multiply by six hundred and forty.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The section reserved for schools
questions.learningObjective: state the origin of the school land reservation
questions.stem: One of the reserved sections in each township was set apart for schools. Which section was it, and what is the significance of the reservation?

options.text: Section twenty-nine, reserved for schools, with section sixteen kept for religious purposes
options.misconception: swaps the school and religion sections

options.text: Section eleven, reserved for schools, with the other three sold at the minimum price
options.misconception: assigns the school share to a section reserved for later disposition

options.text: Section eight, reserved for schools, with the remaining reserved sections sold to settlers
options.misconception: names a different reserved number as the school section

options.text: Section sixteen, reserved for the support of schools, the beginning of the practice of devoting public land to schools

questions.explanation: In each township of the surveyed public domain, section sixteen was reserved for the support of schools, section twenty-nine for religion, and sections eight, eleven, and twenty-six for later disposition by Congress, and two entire townships were reserved in perpetuity for a university. Section sixteen is therefore the school section, and the practice of devoting a fixed share of the public land to schools is the origin of the school land systems that many western states built their school funds on. The second option swaps the school and religion sections, the third assigns the school share to a section that was reserved for later disposition, and the fourth names another of the reserved numbers. Reading the list carefully is the whole skill here, since the numbers are close together and easy to confuse.
questions.hint: List the reserved numbers in order and match each to its stated purpose.

questions.topic: The townships reserved for a university
questions.learningObjective: compute the area reserved for a university
questions.stem: The survey ordinance set apart two entire surveying townships in perpetuity for the support of a university. Each township is six miles square. How many square miles, and how many acres, were set apart in all?

options.text: Seventy-two square miles, which is four hundred and sixty thousand eight hundred acres
options.misconception: adds a zero to the acreage after converting

options.text: Seventy-two square miles, which is four thousand six hundred and eight acres
options.misconception: drops a zero from the conversion factor

options.text: Seventy-two square miles, which is forty-six thousand and eighty acres
Thirty-six square miles, which is twenty-three thousand and forty acres
options.misconception: counts one township rather than two

questions.explanation: Two townships at six miles square each give two times thirty-six, which is seventy-two square miles, and at six hundred and forty acres to a square mile that is seventy-two times six hundred and forty, which is forty-six thousand and eighty acres. The first option has both figures right. The second option counts one township rather than two and so carries the acreage of a single township. The third option has the square miles right and then adds a zero to the converted figure, which is the slip a reader makes when the answer looks too neat to be wrong. The fourth option drops a zero from the conversion factor and multiplies by sixty-four instead of six hundred and forty, and a reader who has lost a place in the conversion will not notice.
questions.hint: Multiply the two townships, then convert square miles into acres at six hundred and forty to the square mile.

questions.topic: The size of an acre in square feet
questions.learningObjective: compute the square footage of a section and of an acre
questions.stem: A survey section is one mile square and contains six hundred and forty acres. A mile is five thousand two hundred and eighty feet. How many square feet does a section contain, and how many square feet does that put in one acre?

options.text: Twenty-seven million eight hundred and seventy-eight thousand four hundred square feet to a section, and six hundred and forty to an acre
options.misconception: reports the number of acres as though it were the square footage of an acre

options.text: Twenty-seven million eight hundred and seventy-eight thousand four hundred square feet to a section, and forty-three thousand five hundred and sixty to an acre
Twenty-seven million eight hundred and seventy-eight thousand four hundred square feet to a section, and forty-three thousand five hundred and sixty thousand to an acre
options.misconception: puts a factor of a thousand into the acre

options.text: Twenty-seven million eight hundred and seventy-eight thousand four hundred square feet to a section, and sixty-eight to an acre
options.misconception: multiplies miles rather than feet

questions.explanation: A mile is five thousand two hundred and eighty feet, so a mile square is five thousand two hundred and eighty multiplied by itself, which is twenty-seven million eight hundred and seventy-eight thousand four hundred square feet. Dividing that by the six hundred and forty acres in the section gives forty-three thousand five hundred and sixty square feet to the acre. The first option therefore has both figures right, and the second figure is the check on the first, because the product of the two answers is the section total. The second option multiplies the acre figure by a thousand, the third option divides the acre figure by the number of acres rather than dividing the section area by the number of acres, and the fourth option reports a count of acres as though it were a count of square feet, which is the same confusion in the other direction.
questions.hint: Square the number of feet in a mile, then divide by the number of acres in the section.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The power to proclaim a national monument
questions.learningObjective: state what the Antiquities Act authorises and on what land
questions.stem: A statute of 1906 lets the President declare national monuments by public proclamation. Which of the following is within it?

options.text: Declaring an object of historic or scientific interest on land owned or controlled by the United States to be a national monument
Declaring a privately owned building to be a national monument, with the owner's agreement
options.misconception: reaches privately owned land with a proclamation

options.text: Taking a private farm into federal ownership by proclamation, without a purchase
options.misconception: treats a proclamation as a means of taking land

options.text: Creating a national park unit by proclamation, with the funds of the legislature
options.misconception: confuses a monument with a unit of the park system

questions.explanation: The statute authorises the President, in his discretion, to declare by public proclamation historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest that are situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Government of the United States to be national monuments, and to reserve as a part of them parcels of land. The condition that the land be owned or controlled by the United States is what rules out the second and third options, since a proclamation reaches land the government already holds and is not a means of taking land it does not. The fourth option confuses two things: a monument is created by proclamation, whereas a unit of the park system is created by an act of the legislature, and the statute says nothing about funds.
questions.hint: Look for the condition about who owns the land on which the object stands.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The limit on the land a monument may reserve
questions.learningObjective: state the size standard in the Antiquities Act
questions.stem: The 1906 statute allows the President to reserve parcels of land as part of a national monument. What limit does it place on those parcels?

options.text: The reserved land may not exceed five hundred acres, whatever the object requires
options.misconception: invents a fixed acreage limit the statute does not state

options.text: The reserved land may not include any land already held by a state or a private owner
options.misconception: states the ownership condition as though it were a size limit

options.text: The reserved land may be whatever area the proclamation needs, with no size standard at all
options.misconception: denies that the statute imposes any size standard

options.text: The limits must in all cases be confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected

questions.explanation: The statute says that the President may reserve as a part of the monument parcels of land, the limits of which in all cases shall be confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected. The standard is therefore functional rather than numerical: the parcel is measured against what the object needs, and the words smallest area and in all cases are what make it a limit rather than a description. A reader who expects a fixed number of acres will invent one, and the five hundred acres in the second option is exactly that, but the statute states no figure at all, which is also why the fourth option is wrong. The third option describes the condition on ownership of the land, which is a different matter from the size of a reservation within land the government already holds.
questions.hint: Ask whether the standard in the statute is a number of acres or a test about what the object needs.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two aims of the park service
questions.learningObjective: state the two aims and the standard in the Organic Act sentence
questions.stem: The statute that created the national park system imposes a duty in a single sentence. What are its two aims and its standard?

options.text: To provide for enjoyment first and to permit whatever alteration the enjoyment requires
options.misconception: puts enjoyment first and lets it justify alteration

options.text: To preserve the land for future use and to leave management to the states in which the units lie
options.misconception: leaves management to the states in which the units lie

options.text: To conserve the scenery, natural and historic objects, and wild life, and to provide for the enjoyment of them, leaving them unimpaired for future generations
To conserve the resources of the system and to keep the number of units as small as possible
options.misconception: describes a different statutory aim altogether

questions.explanation: The statute directs the Secretary, acting through the Director, to promote and regulate the use of the national park system by means and measures that conform to the fundamental purpose of the system units, which purpose is to conserve the scenery, natural and historic objects, and wild life in the system units and to provide for the enjoyment of the scenery, natural and historic objects, and wild life in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations. The sentence carries two aims and one standard, and the standard is attached to the second aim: enjoyment is to be provided in a manner that leaves the resources unimpaired, which is why the third option, which puts enjoyment first and lets it justify alteration, inverts the sentence. The second and fourth options describe something else entirely.
questions.hint: Count the aims in the sentence and ask what the final words qualify.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the unimpaired standard qualifies
questions.learningObjective: identify which part of the duty the standard governs
questions.stem: The statutory sentence contains two aims joined by and to. Which part does the words leaving them unimpaired qualify?

options.text: Only the conservation of scenery, leaving the historic objects and the wild life outside the standard
options.misconception: narrows the standard to scenery alone

options.text: The manner of providing for enjoyment, which is to be carried out by such means as will leave the resources unimpaired
Both aims, so that even conservation itself is qualified by the standard of leaving the resources unimpaired
options.misconception: makes the standard a limit on both aims at once

options.text: Neither aim, because the standard is a statement of aim rather than a condition on the means
options.misconception: denies that the final words are a condition at all

The second option makes the standard a limit on both aims, the third denies that it is a condition at all, and the fourth limits it to scenery although the sentence names the scenery, the natural and historic objects, and the wild life together.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two aims the final words are inside.

questions.topic: The rule about designating wilderness
questions.learningObjective: state the rule governing the designation of wilderness areas
questions.stem: A statute of 1964 established a national wilderness preservation system. What does it say about how federal land becomes wilderness?

options.text: That no federal lands are to be designated as wilderness areas except as provided for in the statute or by a subsequent act of Congress
That the President may designate wilderness by proclamation on any federal land, as for a national monument
options.misconception: borrows the proclamation route from the monument statute

options.text: That any area classified as primitive by the forest service becomes wilderness automatically
options.misconception: treats an administrative classification as a designation

options.text: That a state legislature may designate wilderness within a national forest in its own borders
options.misconception: gives a state legislature power over federal land

questions.explanation: The statute provides for the protection of the designated areas, the preservation of their wilderness character, and the gathering and dissemination of information about their use and enjoyment, and declares that no federal lands shall be designated as wilderness areas except as provided for in the statute or by a subsequent act. The requirement of an act is the point of comparison with the 1906 statute, which allows a monument to be created by proclamation, and the difference between the two routes is one of the clearest contrasts between the two texts. The second option borrows the monument route, the third option treats an administrative classification as a designation, which the statute does not, and the fourth option gives a state legislature a power over federal land that it does not have. A recommendation by the President becomes effective only if so provided by an act of Congress.
questions.hint: Ask what instrument the statute requires before land becomes wilderness.

questions.topic: The uses the wilderness statute withholds
questions.learningObjective: identify the exceptions to the wilderness prohibitions
questions.stem: The wilderness statute bars commercial enterprise, roads, motor vehicles, aircraft landings, and structures within a designated area. What exceptions does it write into that bar?

options.text: Existing private rights, and anything a visitor needs in order to reach a trailhead by vehicle
options.misconception: invents a modern visitor use the exception does not describe

options.text: Nothing, because the statute creates an absolute prohibition with no exception of any kind
options.misconception: denies that the statute has any exception

options.text: Only what a state law permits, because the state law supplies the standard the statute leaves open
options.misconception: invents a state-law standard the statute does not refer to

options.text: Existing private rights, and what is necessary to meet minimum requirements for administering the area, including emergencies of health and safety

questions.explanation: The statute provides that except as specifically provided for in the act, and subject to existing private rights, there shall be no commercial enterprise and no permanent road within a wilderness area, and that except as necessary to meet minimum requirements for the administration of the area, including measures required in emergencies involving the health and safety of persons within the area, there shall be no temporary road, no use of motor vehicles, motorized equipment or motorboats, no landing of aircraft, no other form of mechanical transport, and no structure or installation. So there are two openings in the bar, and both are narrow, which disposes of the third option. The second option is a modern use that the administration exception does not describe, since it is tied to administering the area and to emergencies, and the fourth option invents a state-law standard that the statute does not refer to.
questions.hint: Find the words that follow the list of prohibited uses, and the words that qualify its opening.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The review schedule for primitive areas
questions.learningObjective: compute the review fractions and their acreages
questions.stem: The wilderness statute directed a review of every area classified as primitive, with advice on not less than one third of them within three years, not less than two thirds within seven years, and the remainder within ten years. questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What a procedural requirement can and cannot do
questions.learningObjective: explain what a procedural environmental requirement accomplishes
questions.stem: Explain what an environmental statute that requires an agency to analyse the environmental effects of a major action and to put the analysis in the record can and cannot be relied on to do.

answer.exemplar: The requirement does three things and leaves a fourth to somebody else. First, it forces information: the agency has to state the environmental impact of the proposed action, the adverse effects that cannot be avoided whatever is chosen, and the alternatives, so a decision that would otherwise have been made on a preference has to be made on a record. Second, it opens that record to the public and to comment, because a statement that is filed in the record and referred to in a report is a statement that other people can see and answer, and that is what gives the requirement most of its practical effect. Third, it puts the analysis in front of the decision rather than behind it, which is why the sequence in the statute runs from the proposal to the statement to the decision and not the other way round. What the requirement cannot do is supply the missing judgment. It contains no prohibition and no number, so it does not make a harmful action unlawful, it does not make a cheap action preferable, and it does not decide between two competing goods; all it guarantees is that whoever decides has said out loud what the consequences are. The limitations follow from that character. An agency can satisfy the requirement with a thin analysis, a court may have little standard to review it against, and a decision can be defended on grounds that have nothing to do with the environment provided the analysis was done. That is why the requirement is described as procedural, and why arguments about how far it reaches are usually arguments about what a procedure can achieve rather than about what the statute says. An answer should also notice what the statute itself does about a conflict: it provides that compliance is excused where compliance would be inconsistent with other statutory requirements, which is a conflict rule about the obligations of the agency and not an exemption for the agency that decides the inconsistency.

questions.explanation: The strong answer separates the three effects that follow from a requirement of analysis and disclosure, which are the production of information, the opening of the record to comment, and the placement of the analysis before the decision, from the fourth thing it does not do, which is to supply the judgment the statute leaves to the agency. Because the statute contains neither a prohibition nor a figure, a harmful action is not made unlawful and a cheap action is not made preferable, and a thin analysis can satisfy it. The limitations that follow are the ones a reader should be able to state: the standard for reviewing the analysis is thin, the decision can be defended on other grounds provided the paperwork was done, and the statutory conflict rule is about inconsistent obligations rather than an exemption for the deciding agency.
questions.hint: List what the requirement forces, then list what it leaves to the agency, and check that the statute contains no prohibition and no number.

questions.topic: Setting land aside compared with regulating its use
questions.learningObjective: compare the two federal techniques for protecting land
questions.stem: Compare the two federal techniques for protecting land: setting land aside in a system with its own rules, and regulating the conduct of people who use land. Explain what each is good at and what each cannot do.

answer.exemplar: The two techniques differ in what they act on. Setting land aside changes the legal character of the land itself: once an area is in a wilderness area, the statute withholds a list of uses, commercial enterprise, permanent and temporary roads, motor vehicles, motorized equipment, motorboats, the landing of aircraft, other mechanical transport, and structures and installations, subject to the existing private rights that the statute preserves and to what is necessary to administer the area including emergencies of health and safety. Because the bar attaches to the land, it binds everyone without having to be applied to anyone, and it does not depend on finding a person to regulate. Its weakness is the mirror image: it protects only the land set aside, and it protects it by refusing uses, so it is a poor instrument for a problem that is regional or that is caused by people who never enter the area. The monument power is the same technique with a different trigger, since it too acts by declaring land and withholding uses, and its own weakness is the absence of any stated size limit, which is what invites the argument that a designation may reach further than the object it protects requires. Regulating conduct acts on people rather than on land. The discharge permit programme, for example, authorises a permit for the discharge of a pollutant on conditions drawn from the chapter, caps the term at five years, and allows the permit to be terminated or modified for cause including a violation of a condition, a misrepresentation in the application, or a change in the condition of the water requiring a reduction; the permit conditions for a new source in an area that has not met the national standard require offsetting reductions sufficient to represent reasonable further progress, and the lowest achievable emission rate, and no permit at all where the plan for the area is not being adequately implemented. The strength of this technique is reach: it can operate on a river, an airshed, or a region rather than on a parcel. Its weakness is that it works only if someone applies, and the application, the monitoring, and the enforcement are where it succeeds or fails. The most useful answer ends by noticing that the two are not rivals but stages of the same problem, since the list of reserved sections in each surveyed township, including the section reserved for schools, is an example of the first technique operating on paper and the permit programme is an example of the second operating on a river, and a government serious about a watershed uses both.

questions.explanation: The comparison should turn on what each technique acts on. Setting land aside alters the legal character of the land, which is why a list of uses is withheld by the statute itself and binds everyone without anyone being identified as a target, and the cost of that strength is that it protects only the area set aside and only against the uses named. Regulating conduct leaves the land's character alone and imposes duties on people, which is why it can reach a river or an airshed rather than a parcel, and why its success depends on applications, monitoring, and enforcement. A good answer also names the two statutory safeguards that show each technique working as designed, the smallest-area condition in the monument statute and the cap on a permit term together with the grounds for ending a permit, and it should close by noticing that the reserved school section in each township is the first technique and the discharge permit is the second, so the two are stages of one problem rather than alternatives.
questions.hint: Ask what each technique acts on, the land or the people using it, and then ask what each cannot reach.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the property power covers in its terms
questions.learningObjective: frame the dispute over the breadth of the term property
questions.stem: The property clause speaks of the territory or other property belonging to the United States. What is disputed about the breadth of that term?

options.text: Whether the term includes the airspace above federal land, which no court has considered
options.misconception: raises a question about airspace that nobody has framed

options.text: Whether the term reaches anything at all, since a clause about property cannot confer power
options.misconception: denies the power the clause confers

options.text: Whether the power is confined to the lands and chattels the United States holds, or reaches more broadly, and how far the clause is read is contested
Whether the term is limited to real property, so that a claim about a patent or a copyright falls outside it
options.misconception: narrows the clause to real property only

questions.explanation: The clause says property belonging to the United States, and a long-standing disagreement is about how broadly the word is read and how far the power to dispose of and to make rules reaches over what the government holds, as distinct from the power to regulate conduct. The first option states that disagreement in the form it takes. The second option narrows the clause in a way the text does not support, since a patent or a copyright is a form of property the United States holds and the clause uses no limiting adjective. The third option is a question no one has framed, and the fourth option denies the power the clause plainly confers, which is the reading the framers rejected when they adopted the clause in place of a proposal that gave Congress power over the lands of the individual states.
questions.hint: Ask whether the dispute is about the word property or about the reach of a power the clause states.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The quarter section and the forty-acre piece
questions.learningObjective: compute the sizes produced by dividing a section
questions.stem: A survey section of six hundred and forty acres is divided in the usual way into quarter sections, and a quarter section is divided into four pieces. How many acres is a quarter section, and how many is each of the sixteen pieces?

options.text: Six hundred and forty acres to a quarter section and one hundred and sixty to a piece
options.misconception: calls the whole section a quarter and moves a level down

options.text: One hundred and sixty acres to a quarter section and forty acres to a piece
Three hundred and twenty acres to a quarter section and eighty acres to a piece
options.misconception: halves a section instead of quartering it

options.text: One hundred and sixty acres to a quarter section and twenty acres to a piece
options.misconception: divides a quarter section into eight

questions.explanation: A section of six hundred and forty acres divides into four quarter sections, so a quarter section is six hundred and forty divided by four, which is one hundred and sixty acres. A quarter section then divides into four pieces, so each of the sixteen pieces in a section is one hundred and sixty divided by four, which is forty acres. The first option has both figures right, and the second figure is a check on the first, since sixteen pieces of forty acres come to six hundred and forty. The second option halves a section instead of quartering it, the third option divides a quarter section into eight rather than four, and the fourth option calls the whole section a quarter and then moves a level down.
questions.hint: Divide six hundred and forty by four, then divide the result by four again.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Excluding land from critical habitat
questions.learningObjective: state the exclusion provision and its backstop
questions.stem: The endangered species statute allows an area to be excluded from critical habitat on a stated weighing, and then adds a limit on that power. What is the limit?

options.text: That no area may be excluded if, on the best scientific and commercial data available, failure to designate it would result in the extinction of a species
That no area may be excluded unless every other area in the range has first been designated
options.misconception: invents an order of designations

options.text: That the weighing of benefits may be made only by the legislature and never by the Secretary
options.misconception: moves the weighing to the legislature

options.text: That no exclusion is available once any notice of a proposed designation has been published
options.misconception: invents a bar arising from publication of a notice

questions.explanation: The Secretary may exclude any area from critical habitat if he determines that the benefits of the exclusion outweigh the benefits of specifying that area as part of the critical habitat, unless he determines, on the best scientific and commercial data available, that the failure to designate that area as critical habitat will result in the extinction of a species. So the weighing is permitted and the backstop is an extinction test, and the first option states the backstop. The second option invents an order of designations, the third option moves the weighing to the legislature, which the provision does not do, and the fourth option invents a bar that arises from the publication of a notice, which the provision nowhere mentions.
questions.hint: Find the words unless that follow the weighing, and ask what determination they turn on.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who draws the boundary of each designation
questions.learningObjective: compare how each boundary is established
questions.stem: A monument is created by proclamation and a wilderness area only by an act. What follows about who decides the boundary of each?

options.text: That in both cases the boundary is drawn by the agency and confirmed afterwards by the legislature
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the instruments in both cases

options.text: That in both cases the boundary is fixed by the original survey of the township and cannot be altered
options.misconception: confuses the survey grid with a designation

options.text: That the legislature draws a monument boundary and the President draws a wilderness boundary, the reverse of the instruments
options.misconception: swaps the two instruments around

options.text: That the proclamation sets a monument's own limits, while a wilderness boundary is fixed by what the act itself describes

questions.explanation: The proclamation that creates a monument is itself the instrument that sets its limits, because the statute allows the President to reserve parcels as part of it and to confine them to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects, so the limits are described in the proclamation. A wilderness area is different, because the statute makes the designation effective only as provided by an act, and the act is what describes the area, so the boundary is fixed by the legislature. The second option reverses the direction in both cases, the third confuses the survey grid with a designation, and the fourth swaps the instruments in a way neither statute supports.
questions.hint: Ask which document names the boundary in each case, and follow from the instrument to the description.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whether built structures are covered by the conservation aim
questions.learningObjective: frame the dispute over the reach of the conservation duty
questions.stem: The park service statute directs the agency to conserve the scenery, natural and historic objects, and wild life. A recurring dispute concerns the built environment. What is the dispute?

options.text: Whether the statute requires every building in a unit to be removed within a fixed period
options.misconception: invents a removal requirement and a period

options.text: Whether the enjoyment the statute speaks of may be provided at a profit, which the statute forbids
options.misconception: invents a prohibition on profit

options.text: Whether the duty to conserve the scenery reaches the design of the buildings the agency itself erects, which some read as covered and others read as outside the words
Whether the statute allows the agency to sell any of the buildings it has built inside a unit
options.misconception: invents a power of sale out of this sentence

questions.explanation: The dispute is about the reach of a single word. The duty is to conserve the scenery, and the question is whether a building the agency constructs is part of the scenery whose conservation the statute requires, so that its design is constrained, or whether the duty attaches only to what is already there and leaves the new construction to the other half of the sentence. The first option states that argument, which is a real disagreement about the text rather than a settled point. The second option invents a power of sale that no one claims to read out of this sentence, the third invents a removal requirement and a period, and the fourth invents a prohibition on profit, which the statute does not address at all.
questions.hint: Locate the single word the argument turns on and ask whether new construction falls inside it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Land ownership and the water running over it
questions.learningObjective: state how ownership and appropriation interact
questions.stem: Someone owns land beside a river and someone else claims a right to divert the water. What decides which claim prevails?

options.text: The federal government, which allocates all water in the states it owns land in
options.misconception: makes the federal government allocate water within a state

options.text: The system the state applies and the priority rules within it, and in addition any right the United States reserved when it took land in the area
Whoever owns the land beside the river, in every state and under every system
options.misconception: states the riparian rule as though it were universal

options.text: Whoever posted the earliest claim, whether or not the water was ever put to use
options.misconception: treats a mere claim as perfecting a right

questions.explanation: The answer is that water rights in the states are governed by the system each state applies, prior appropriation in most of the west and the riparian rule in the east, and by the priority rules inside that system, and that a claim by the United States to water for land it holds sits on top of both because the reservation doctrine gives it a quantity needed for the irrigable portions of the reserved land. The first option names all three of those things. The second option states the riparian rule as though it were universal, which it is not, and the third option states the priority rule as though a mere claim perfected it, which it does not in either system, since an appropriative right requires actual use and a riparian right requires land ownership. The fourth option is wrong twice, because the federal government allocates water between states and does not allocate water within a state.
questions.hint: Ask which system the state applies, and then ask what priority rule operates inside it.
